Sounds & science
A WORLD ABOVE YOU

One continuous climb.

Start on the pavement. Scroll upward through 66 illustrated discoveries from around Earth. Slide the window glass, brush away mist, or trace the water directly on the illustrations.

Five height bands share the same scroll length, with 13, 13, 13, 13 and 14 discoveries. Heights change logarithmically between stops so each fact has room to breathe. The figures compare places across Earth, not one geographic elevator shaft.

Heights include example listening positions, elevations, structure heights, flight records and length comparisons; detailed datums are kept in Sounds & science. A whale or kelp pictured at a matching body length is not flying above the ground.

The short answers distinguish real subject recordings from listening examples; Sounds & science lists every origin and adaptation. Scene fades are illustrative, not exact audible ranges or calibrated decibels. Some upper scenes use recorded listening examples; others stay quiet.

The compact readouts use a standard atmosphere and a geometric horizon model. They describe an idealised altitude above sea level, not the weather at a pictured landmark. Below water’s triple-point pressure, there is no stable liquid-water boiling point.
